extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of the natural sciences; readers learning scientific method and experimental design (philosophy of science audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for correct scientific observation and experimental practice: how to account for external conditions, avoid inference fallacies, evaluate negative evidence, and design experiments (isolation of variables, exclusion of indifferent circumstances, dealing with practical limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: External Conditions of Correct Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before we proceed to draw inferences from any series of recorded facts, we must take care to ascertain perfectly, if possible, the external conditions under which the facts are brought to our notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for prejudice of the observing mind, defective senses, and circumstances that cause one kind of event to come more frequently to notice than another. The difference between numbers of objects existing and numbers coming to notice must be taken into account before making inferences (illustrated by comet-observation bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for limited sphere of observation / sampling bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When we attempt to estimate the numbers of objects which may have existed, we must make large allowances for the limited sphere of our observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for absence of observers in regions (e.g., southern hemisphere), low probability of seeing a large fraction of objects near our system, and temporal/spatial observational limits. Examples: proportions of hyperbolic comets, vastly larger unseen populations (Kepler's comparison to fishes), and meteor counts. Adjust inferences to reflect observational reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and survivorship bias in historical/geological records
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious fallacies may arise from overlooking the inevitable conditions under which the records of past events are brought to our notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only durable objects (flint implements, bronze) commonly survive; comparative abundance in museums does not reflect original abundance (e.g., bronze vs iron). Recognize that relics are exceptional; geological and archaeological records are biased toward durable parts (bones, shells), and many forms (infusoria) may be entirely lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider rarity and improbability of extraordinary events
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be conjunctions or terrestrial events of such unusual magnitude and such extreme rarity that we can neither expect to witness them nor readily to comprehend their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probability reasoning (Laplace) to temper inferences and mistrust overconfidence. Recognize that rare events (great storms, volcanic eruptions, unique astronomical conjunctions) may lie outside our observational record, so absence in records does not imply impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent Sequence of Events — four modes of misleading succession (de Morgan)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no less than four modes in which one event may seem to follow or be connected with another, without being really so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Our perception of A may cause B (mental causation) — e.g., prophecies or presentiments producing their own fulfilment. 2) A may make our perception of B follow which would otherwise happen unnoticed (external observation bias) — e.g., hot summers yielding more comet discoveries because skies are clear. 3) Our perception of A may make our perception of B follow (attention bias) — e.g., noticing clouds when the moon is full because both attract attention. 4) B may be the antecedent event but perception of A (a consequent sign) is necessary to bring B to notice (indicator-dependence) — e.g., atmospheric currents only known when cumulus clouds form. Always consider these modes to avoid false causal inferences; examples provided (moon/cloud fallacy, comet tails, meteor visibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Arguments from Non-observation (general caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-observation of a phenomenon is not generally to be taken as proving its non-occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret experience affirmatively; many phenomena (sounds, heat rays, minute organisms, worlds) may escape detection. Historical examples show negative inductions often unsafe (discoveries of Ceres, Eozoon Canadense, deep-sea organisms). Do not infer non-existence from mere absence of observation without further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force of negative evidence depends on detectability and search extent
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that a negative argument founded on the non-observation of an object shall have any considerable force, it must be shown to be probable that the object, if existent, would have been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative conclusions are stronger when (a) the object would be readily detectable if present, (b) the search has been sufficiently extensive (e.g., large terrestrial animals), and (c) alternatives are limited. For small or hard-to-detect objects (microscopic forms, deep-sea life), negative evidence carries less weight. If a specific claim includes time/place, targeted observation can disprove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental aim: ascertain precise antecedent conditions (A = AX formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our object in inductive investigation is to ascertain exactly the group of circumstances or conditions which being present, a certain other group of phenomena will follow. If A denotes antecedent and X subsequent phenomena, the objective is to discover a law of the form A = AX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame experiments to identify which precise conditions (and combinations) produce the effect. Recognize that circumstances are numerous and an exhaustive listing is required in principle; use this formulation to guide experimental design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: remove one condition at a time; isolate variables and test eliminations
rubrics_metrics.description: The great method of experiment consists in removing, one at a time, each of those conditions which may be imagined to have an influence on the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by rubbing sticks: prepare vacuo to test air, make surrounding bodies ice-cold to test conduction, etc. Proceed by eliminating candidate conditions until the sole requisite condition remains. Use controlled variation and targeted exclusion to identify causal conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test conditions both in presence and absence of other conditions (check interactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must not assume the conditions to be independent; the effect of the absence of each condition should be tried both in the presence and absence of every other condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For antecedents A, B, C, D, test combinations (ABCD, ABCd, ABcD, etc.). Interactions may change how a condition operates (branching of inquiry). Practical combinatorial explosion makes full coverage impossible, but the logical ideal is to test interactions to avoid incorrect independence assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impossibility of exhaustive experimentation — use tact, experience, and analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect and exhaustive experimentation would consist in examining natural phenomena in all their possible combinations ... but such exhaustive investigation is practically impossible because the number of requisite experiments would be immensely great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because exhaustive combination-testing is impracticable (grows as powers of two), experimenters must rely on insight, tact, analogy, and knowledge of which conditions have been important in like cases to select the most promising experiments. Examples: Newton's missed discovery until slit was used; use analogy to focus tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware unknown conditions and practical difficulties in altering single factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A very treacherous source of error is the existence of unknown conditions, which of course we cannot remove except by accident. It is often impossible to alter one condition without altering others at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that unknown or unmodifiable factors can confound experiments. Design experiments aware of coupling between conditions and the possibility that critical factors remain unnoticed (Faraday's Lycopodium/air example). Maintain humility about completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of Indifferent Circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The detection and exclusion of indifferent circumstances is a work of importance, because it allows the concentration of attention upon circumstances which contain the principal condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether obvious antecedents actually influence the phenomenon; if indifference is shown, focus on form/structure rather than material (examples: Brewster showing iridescent colours depend on surface form not chemical nature; diffraction fringes independent of material or edge form; Faraday showing the nature of poles is indifferent in electrolysis). Use empirical trials to demonstrate indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific weight of negative/inductive arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The force of negative arguments varies by domain: in geology or widely surveyed domains negative conclusions may be strong, while in microscopical or mathematically open domains they are weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: geology—absence of large terrestrial animals is credible after extensive search; mathematics—many failed attempts do not prove impossibility because alternative constructions may exist (trisecting the angle example). Adjust standards of inference according to domain and the number of possible alternatives.
